action_criteria.expected_evidence: Selective midbrain atrophy (hummingbird and morning glory signs, midbrain-to-pons diameter ratio 0.47) with preserved pons, cerebellum and putamina; mild frontal atrophy; Fazekas 1
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI to exclude a structural, vascular or atypical-parkinsonism cause
action_criteria.rationale: MRI excludes vascular lesions, NPH and mass, and shows the midbrain atrophy that supports PSP and the pontine and putaminal signs of MSA; midbrain atrophy is supportive, not required, for PSP [Hoglinger_2017]

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Dysexecutive profile: FAB 8/18, Stroop z -2.8, Trail Making B discontinued, FAS 8 words, with preserved recall (CVLT-3 11/16), naming and visuoconstruction; apathy scale 42
action_criteria.label: Neuropsychological battery to characterize the frontal cognitive and behavioural change
action_criteria.rationale: Personality change, an applause sign and MoCA 20/30 raise frontal cognitive dysfunction; a battery documents the dysexecutive profile and gives a baseline [Hoglinger_2017]

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Additive hypotension of amlodipine with levodopa (lying and standing blood pressure at each step); calcium carbonate reduces levothyroxine absorption
action_criteria.label: Medication review before increasing levodopa
action_criteria.rationale: Amlodipine adds to levodopa's hypotensive effect in a patient who falls, and her calcium and levothyroxine doses must be separated; no dopamine antagonist is on the list

prohibited_recommendations: Do not prescribe metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, haloperidol or other centrally acting D2-blocking antiemetics or antipsychotics; if an antipsychotic is needed, use quetiapine or clozapine
Do not prescribe sedating drugs that add to fall risk (benzodiazepines, sedating antihistamines, centrally acting anticholinergics such as trihexyphenidyl)
required_recommendations: Diagnose probable PSP-RS (MDS 2017): O1 vertical supranuclear gaze palsy (downgaze about 10 and upgaze about 15 degrees, full vertical oculocephalic range) with P1 repeated unprovoked backward falls within 3 years (8 falls in 18 months); dysarthria and dysphagia are supportive clinical clues (levodopa resistance cannot yet be stated: 600 mg/day for 4 weeks is short of a trial of at least 1000 mg/day for a month), and the midbrain atrophy is a supportive imaging feature [Hoglinger_2017]
Refer to speech and language therapy for a swallowing assessment (instrumental study if needed) and texture modification of liquids, because she coughs and chokes on thin liquids
Fall prevention: physiotherapy for balance and gait with a suitable walking aid, a home safety assessment, and review of bone protection given her osteoporosis
Complete an adequate levodopa trial: increase to up to 1000 mg/day as tolerated for 4 to 8 weeks, with lying and standing blood pressure at each step, and taper it if there is no benefit
Discuss the diagnosis, prognosis and advance care planning (including future decisions on feeding) with the patient and her husband, and offer palliative care involvement

avoided_actions.rationale: CSF analysis has no role in the diagnosis of PSP and would not change management here
No cardiac symptom or sign; the falls are backward falls from postural instability, without loss of consciousness
No syncope or palpitations; rhythm monitoring would not explain the backward falls
A DaTscan does not separate PD from MSA or PSP [Marshall_2009]
Formal autonomic testing is not part of the PSP work-up; bedside orthostatic blood pressure is normal
Tilt testing is not part of the PSP work-up; bedside orthostatic blood pressure is normal and the falls are not syncopal

differential.key_features: Downward vertical supranuclear gaze palsy is an MDS absolute exclusion; no tremor, symmetric axial-predominant rigidity, early unprovoked backward falls and no benefit from 600 mg/day levodopa
No asymmetric apraxia, cortical sensory loss, alien limb or limb dystonia; symmetric signs
Personality change and disinhibition fit, but vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, early backward falls and midbrain atrophy define PSP; frontal atrophy is mild
No visual hallucinations or cognitive fluctuations; the vertical supranuclear gaze palsy and early unprovoked backward falls are not DLB features
No orthostatic hypotension (148/88 to 142/84), no urinary failure or cerebellar signs; pons, cerebellar peduncles and putamina preserved on MRI
Only Fazekas 1 periventricular change; no basal ganglia or brainstem infarcts

key_clinical_evidence: Vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, downgaze more than upgaze (O1), with a full vertical oculocephalic range and square-wave jerks
Repeated unprovoked backward falls beginning 18 months ago (P1), with no compensatory step on the pull test
Symmetric axial-predominant rigidity with retrocollis, no tremor, and no clear benefit from 600 mg/day levodopa for 4 weeks (short of an adequate trial, so levodopa resistance is not yet established)
Frontal behavioural change (irritability, loss of empathy, impulsivity), applause sign, spastic dysarthria and dysphagia to thin liquids
MRI midbrain atrophy (hummingbird and morning glory signs, midbrain-to-pons diameter ratio 0.47) is supportive, not required [Hoglinger_2017]
Fall prevention and dysphagia management are the main management priorities

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Downward vertical supranuclear gaze palsy is an MDS absolute exclusion for PD, and repeated unprovoked falls within 3 years are a PSP core feature (P1): probable PSP-RS
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor toward repeating a levodopa trial as if PD

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Orthostatic testing was negative and the exam shows 148/88 to 142/84 mmHg; the falls are backward falls from postural instability
red_herrings.data_point: Falls initially attributed to amlodipine-related orthostatic hypotension
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute the falls to a medication side effect

interactions: Amlodipine lowers standing blood pressure and levodopa can lower it further: measure lying and standing blood pressure at each levodopa dose step.
Calcium carbonate reduces levothyroxine absorption: take levothyroxine at least 4 hours apart from calcium.
general.summary: No interacting dopamine antagonist on the list. Amlodipine with levodopa: additive hypotension. Calcium carbonate with levothyroxine: separate doses.
warnings: Benzodiazepines, sedating antihistamines and centrally acting anticholinergics add sedation, confusion and fall risk in older patients.
Levodopa: nausea and postural hypotension are the common dose-limiting effects at higher doses.

additional_observations: No acute infarct on diffusion-weighted imaging
No ventriculomegaly out of proportion to sulcal atrophy

metadata.diagnostic_challenge: Differentiating progressive supranuclear palsy from Parkinson disease in a patient referred with 'atypical PD' after poor levodopa response, requiring recognition of vertical gaze palsy, early falls, and characteristic imaging
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Referred as atypical PD after a failed levodopa trial, the patient meets probable PSP-RS on examination: the agent must recognise the vertical supranuclear gaze palsy and the early unprovoked backward falls, and not blame the falls on amlodipine. One required criterion (MRI).
metadata.educational_value: Teaches recognition of PSP-Richardson syndrome cardinal features including vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, early backward falls, axial-predominant rigidity, poor levodopa response, and the hummingbird sign on MRI
metadata.revision_reason: October 2026 review round: plans/PD.md. Literature criterion deleted; medication review optional and rebuilt (amlodipine, calcium with levothyroxine); levodopa arithmetic corrected; MMSE and MoCA items made to sum; examiner comparisons with PD removed from the exam; MRI restructured; symmetric DaTscan stored as waste; neuropsychology impression rewritten; PSP musts and differential rewritten.
teaching_points: Vertical supranuclear gaze palsy (especially downgaze) is the hallmark of PSP-Richardson syndrome
Early backward falls within the first 18 months should trigger consideration of PSP over PD
The oculocephalic reflex distinguishes supranuclear from nuclear gaze palsy
Hummingbird sign and morning glory sign on MRI are characteristic of PSP
Poor levodopa response at adequate doses should prompt reconsideration of PD diagnosis
DaTscan is abnormal in PSP as well as PD — it does not distinguish between them
Dysphagia with aspiration is a major morbidity and mortality concern in PSP

patient.history_present_illness: Dr. Priya Sharma is a 72-year-old right-handed retired university professor of comparative literature who is referred to the neurology movement disorders clinic by her primary care physician for evaluation of 'atypical Parkinson's disease' after failing to respond to levodopa therapy. Her husband, who accompanies her, provides a detailed history. Approximately 18 months ago, she began having recurrent falls. The falls have been predominantly BACKWARD — she falls straight back when standing from a chair, when turning around, or when bumped slightly from the front. She has had 8 falls in total, 3 of which required emergency department evaluation. Fortunately, she has not sustained fractures, but she did require stitches for a scalp laceration from one backward fall. Her PCP initially attributed the falls to orthostatic hypotension related to her amlodipine, but orthostatic testing was negative. Around the same time, she began having difficulty looking down. She cannot see the food on her plate without tilting her entire head down, has great difficulty navigating stairs because she cannot look at her feet, and struggles to read a book in her lap. Her husband notes that her eyes seem 'stuck' and she has to move her whole head to look at things rather than moving her eyes. Her speech has become progressively slow, harsh, and strained over the past year — different from the quiet voice she has heard in friends with Parkinson's disease. She has had increasing difficulty swallowing thin liquids, with frequent coughing and choking when drinking water or coffee. Her husband has noticed personality changes — she has become more irritable, less empathetic (she showed no emotional response when their grandson was hospitalized), and more impulsive (interrupts conversations, makes rude comments). She has never had any tremor. Her PCP started carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 TID three months ago with no improvement. The dose was increased to two tablets of 25/100 three times daily (600 mg/day levodopa) for the past 4 weeks, again with no clear benefit. The lack of response prompted referral to neurology. She denies visual hallucinations, urinary incontinence, or significant memory complaints (though her husband notes she sometimes forgets recent conversations).

neurological_exam.additional: No orthostatic hypotension (BP supine 148/88, standing 142/84). No inspiratory stridor.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing intact bilaterally without dysmetria. Heel-to-shin mildly slow bilaterally. Rapid alternating movements moderately slowed bilaterally, symmetric.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light. Extraocular movements: square-wave jerks on primary gaze. Voluntary vertical gaze severely restricted: downgaze limited to approximately 10 degrees, upgaze to approximately 15 degrees. Horizontal saccades are slow but achieve full range. Oculocephalic manoeuvre (doll's eyes): full vertical range of eye movement when the head is passively flexed and extended. Blepharospasm present. Procerus sign: deeply furrowed brow with a fixed, astonished expression. Hearing intact bilaterally. Palate elevates symmetrically but patient coughs when drinking water during exam (suggesting mild dysphagia). Tongue midline without fasciculations.
neurological_exam.gait: Erect posture, not stooped. Gait is slow and stiff-legged with wide base. Reduced stride length. Arms held rigidly at sides with minimal swing. Pronounced postural instability on pull test: falls backward without any compensatory stepping (examiner must catch her). Turns require 6-8 steps, en bloc. No freezing of gait. Cannot perform tandem gait.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person, place, and situation. Oriented to month and year but not exact date (3 days off). MMSE 25/30: lost 2 points on serial sevens (2 errors), 1 point on recall (2/3 words, third retrieved with category cue), 1 point on orientation (date) and 1 point on the pentagon copy. MoCA 20/30: visuospatial/executive 3/5 (trail-making 0/1, cube 1/1, clock 2/3), naming 3/3, attention 5/6 (serial 7s with 2 errors), language 2/3 (3 F-words in 60 seconds), abstraction 0/2, delayed recall 2/5 (1 more with cue), orientation 5/6 (date). Speech is slow, harsh, and strained (spastic dysarthria). Personality change noted by husband: more irritable, impatient, less empathetic, occasional impulsive responses. Applause sign positive (clapped 8 times, unable to stop at 3). Motor impersistence on tongue protrusion (could not maintain for 15 seconds).
neurological_exam.motor: Normal bulk throughout. Tone: prominent axial rigidity (neck and trunk) with relatively mild appendicular rigidity at wrists. Retrocollis present (neck held in extension). Bradykinesia present bilaterally, approximately symmetric, on finger tapping and hand opening-closing. No resting tremor observed during 20-minute observation. No action tremor. Strength 5/5 throughout all extremities. No pronator drift.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 3+ at patellar bilaterally, 2+ elsewhere. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. Palmomental reflex present bilaterally. Grasp reflexes present bilaterally. No Hoffmann sign.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch and pinprick intact throughout. Vibration sense intact at great toes bilaterally. Proprioception intact. No cortical sensory deficits (no alien limb, no asymmetric apraxia, no cortical sensory loss).
